# What happens after you submit your libraries {#sec-after-submission}

You have made RNA-seq libraries, checked them on a TapeStation or
Bioanalyzer, quantified them, and handed them to the sequencing core. A few
days later you get an email with a folder of `.fastq.gz` files. This chapter
covers what happened in between and what is in those files, because
almost every decision later in the pipeline depends on it.

## A library, in one picture

An RNA-seq library is a tube of short DNA fragments. Each fragment is a piece
of your RNA (converted to cDNA) with **adapters** ligated on both ends:

```
5'-[P5][i5 index][Read 1 primer site]=====cDNA insert=====[Read 2 primer site][i7 index][P7]-3'
```

- **P5 / P7** let the fragment stick to the flow cell.
- **Index (barcode) sequences** (i7, and on dual-indexed kits i5) are short tags that are
  different for each of your samples, so many libraries can share one lane.
- **The insert** is the part you care about: a fragment of your RNA, usually
  150 to 400 bp long.

## Sequencing: reading the fragment from both ends

On an Illumina instrument (NovaSeq, NextSeq), each fragment is copied into a
cluster on the flow cell and read one base at a time.
In **paired-end** sequencing the machine reads the insert from one end
(**Read 1**, R1), then from the other end (**Read 2**, R2). bagPipes'
`RNApipe` expects paired-end data.

```
insert:     5'-ACGTTGCA..............................GGATCCTA-3'
Read 1:        ACGTTGCA.......>                                 (from the left)
Read 2:                                  <.......TAGGATCC       (from the right, reverse complement)
```

Two numbers describe a run:

- **Read length**, written as `2x50`, `2x100` or `2x150`: how many bases are read
  from each end.
- **Depth**: how many read pairs you got per sample. For gene-level
  differential expression, 20 to 30 million pairs per sample is a common
  target; the bagPipes test data has only 100,000 so it runs fast.

::: {.callout-note}
## What happens when the insert is shorter than the read?

If the insert is 80 bp but the machine reads 150 bp, it reads through the
whole insert and into the adapter on the other side. Those adapter bases are
not from your RNA and will not match the genome. Removing them is the main
job of [trimming](trimming.qmd).
:::

## Demultiplexing: one lane, many samples

The sequencer reads the index sequences too. The core facility then runs a
program (usually Illumina's `bcl2fastq` or `bcl-convert`) that sorts the reads
by index into one pair of files per sample. This is **demultiplexing**. It is
why the sample sheet you give the core, with the index you used for
each tube, has to be right: if two samples share an index, their reads end up mixed together and cannot be separated.

The output is named in Illumina's style:

```
IMGL_RNA_MGL_F_Ab_24h_S_1-1-1_S4_R1_001.fastq.gz
└────── your sample name ─────┘└S#┘└R1┘└001┘
                                sample  read  chunk
                                number  1 or 2
```

Sometimes a sample is sequenced on several lanes and you get `_L001_`,
`_L002_` in the names. bagPipes treats each samplesheet row as **one pair of
FASTQ files**, so combine lanes first (for example with `cat` on the `.gz`
files, R1 with R1 and R2 with R2, in the same order).

## Strandedness: which strand did the read come from?

Genes sit on both strands of the genome. A **stranded** library keeps track
of which strand the RNA came from; an **unstranded** library does not.

Most stranded kits today (Illumina TruSeq Stranded, NEB Ultra II Directional,
and others) use the **dUTP method**. The practical result:

- **Read 1 is the reverse complement of the RNA** (antisense).
- **Read 2 has the same sequence as the RNA** (sense).

You need to know this later, when you build strand-specific signal tracks
([Signal tracks](signal-tracks.qmd)). Salmon will also detect the library
type for you and report it ([Salmon](salmon.qmd)).

## What you should get back from the core

| Thing | Why you need it |
|---|---|
| `*_R1_001.fastq.gz` and `*_R2_001.fastq.gz` per sample | The data |
| Read length and instrument | To choose settings and interpret QC |
| Library kit (stranded? which one?) | To interpret strand-specific tracks |
| Reads per sample (often a demultiplexing report) | To see early whether a library failed |
| `md5` checksums | To confirm files were not corrupted while copying |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. You sequenced `2x100` and your average insert is 120 bp. Will Read 1 and
   Read 2 overlap? Will either read run into adapter?
2. Why can't the core separate two samples that were given the same index?
3. In a dUTP library, a gene on the **+** strand produces reads. Which strand
   does Read 1 align to?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. Yes, they overlap by 80 bp (100 + 100 − 120). Neither runs into adapter,
   because each read (100 bp) is shorter than the insert (120 bp). Inserts
   shorter than 100 bp would.
2. Demultiplexing sorts reads only by the index sequence, so reads with the
   same index look identical to the software.
3. The **−** strand. Read 1 is antisense to the RNA, and the RNA came from
   the + strand.
:::
:::
